The breast slide file was too large to open, so this page is built from the doctor's notes (green) and every gift (red). Aldughaither's Final summary has no breast-cancer chapter.

Breast examination

  • Inspection: skin oedema/peau d'orange, nipple position (normal vs retracted), visible masses/skin changes.
  • Palpation with the palmar surface of the fingers, systematically by 4 quadrants or clock face; superficial (tenderness) then deep palpation.
  • Describe any mass: side + exact location/quadrant/clock position, size, mobility, fixation to skin or deep tissues, tenderness. Finish one breast, then the other.
  • Axilla: right axilla with the left hand and vice versa, arm supported. Nodes: number, size, discrete vs matted, mobile vs fixed.
  • Metastatic examination: abdomen (ascites, organomegaly) and back/skeleton (bone metastases).
  • Most common presentation of breast cancer in Saudi Arabia → painless breast mass. 436

Investigations

  • Breast assessment relies on radiology + biopsy; blood tests matter less initially. Imaging: ultrasound, mammography, MRI.
  • Palpable 3-cm mass after history & exam → imaging, then biopsy 437 ×3; mammogram is ordered to look for microcalcifications 438; young woman with bloody discharge → ultrasound. 438
  • 70-year-old man with an ulcerating breast mass and axillary nodes → initial step mammogram (then biopsy) — not excision or antibiotics. 438 ×5

BI-RADS

CategoryMeaningAction
0IncompleteAdditional imaging
1NegativeRoutine follow-up
2BenignRoutine follow-up
3Probably benign (< 2% malignancy)Short-interval follow-up (3–6 months)
4SuspiciousBiopsy
5Highly suspiciousBiopsy
6Biopsy-proven malignancy—

Biopsy

  • Core needle biopsy: palpable → clinical core under local; non-palpable → US-guided, stereotactic (mammography-guided), or MRI-guided (most difficult).
  • Never excise an undiagnosed mass first — if malignant, the oncological margins won't have been taken and surgery must be repeated.
  • Best initial diagnostic step for a breast mass → core biopsy (not FNA or surgery). 434 ×2
Core biopsy tells youDetails
1. DiagnosisBenign vs malignant
2. Histological typeDuctal (most common), lobular (2nd); mucinous, papillary, medullary
3. Grade1 well · 2 intermediate · 3 poorly differentiated — grade ≠ stage
4. ER, PRBenefit from hormonal therapy
5. HER2~15%, aggressive; HER2-targeted therapy
6. Ki-67Proliferation: 5% slow vs 90% aggressive
  • Most common type of breast cancer → invasive ductal carcinoma ("intraductal" in the recall). 437

Biological subtypes

SubtypeER/PRHER2Grade / Ki-67Behaviour & systemic treatment
Luminal A+−Grade 1, Ki-67 low (≤ 10%)Best prognosis → hormonal therapy alone
Luminal BER+, usually PR+±Grade 2–3, Ki-67 higherMore aggressive → chemo + hormonal
HER2-positiveVariable+—Aggressive → chemo + anti-HER2 (trastuzumab) ± endocrine
Triple-negative−−—Very aggressive (young) → chemotherapy only
  • ER−, PR−, HER2+ → trastuzumab (Herceptin) (tamoxifen, letrozole and goserelin need ER+). 442
  • 95-year-old, devastating comorbidities, ulcerating T3N0M0 luminal A (ER/PR ~100%, Ki-67 5%, grade 1) → hormonal therapy only. 439 ×3

Staging & the metastatic screen

StageMeaning
I–IIEarly: small/localized ± limited nodes
IIILocally advanced, confined to breast + regional nodes
IVMetastatic — 5-year survival < 18%; ~95% non-surgical (chemo, hormonal, targeted)
Metastatic screen after a positive biopsy — CT chest, abdomen, pelvis + bone scan — before surgery or chemo. Commonly forgotten OSCE step. Sequence: history → exam → mammogram/US → biopsy → metastatic screen → staging → management.
  • Breast cancer 5 years ago, now 3 weeks of neck pain without trauma → spinal MRI (bone metastasis/cord compression). 439
  • Metastatic (brain + bone) triple-negative cancer → keyed palliative care (the doctor: stage IV is treated systemically — palliative chemotherapy; no breast surgery). 436
  • Single most important prognostic factor → number of involved axillary nodes. 429 ×3

Inflammatory breast cancer

  • Rare, extremely aggressive (more than typical TNBC). Mimics an abscess: redness, heat, swelling, fever. Antibiotics may seem to help (the inflammatory reaction settles) → false reassurance.
  • If treating a presumed abscess, review every ~2 weeks; non-resolving or enlarging → biopsy.
  • "Cellulitis" recurring 5 times despite antibiotics → skin biopsy. 441

Treatment

Systemic therapy

  • Hormonal (oral, ER+ only, 5–10 years) · HER2-targeted (IV every ~3 weeks) · chemotherapy (IV every ~3 weeks, 4/6/8 cycles — strong indications: TNBC, HER2+, many luminal B).
  • Triple-negative with one positive axillary node → neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then surgery. 442 ×4
  • Locally advanced (stage III, skin involvement, 3 nodes) invasive ductal carcinoma → neoadjuvant chemotherapy first. 436 ×3

Locoregional therapy

  • Breast-conserving surgery = lumpectomy (≈ 1–1.5 cm margin) + radiotherapy. If RT can't be given → mastectomy.
Lumpectomy unsuitable → mastectomyWhy
Multicentric / multifocal diseaseCan't remove adequately while conserving
Extensive DCIS
Large tumor in a small breastNeoadjuvant chemo may shrink it
BRCA1/2Relative contraindication
PregnancyNo RT during pregnancy
Previous chest/breast radiationRepeat RT unsafe (toxicity, secondary sarcoma)
Collagen vascular disease (lupus)Flares with RT
  • Practical barriers to RT (cost, distance, staying 1–1.5 months) — an informed patient may choose mastectomy.
  • ER+ cancer in a 65-year-old with previous bilateral breast radiation for Hodgkin's → simple mastectomy (can't re-irradiate). 442
  • Breast mass with clinically and radiologically benign-looking nodes → breast-conserving surgery + sentinel node biopsy. 439 ×3
  • Retroareolar ER/PR+ HER2− mass with nipple retraction, node-negative (recall without choices) → central lumpectomy removing the nipple–areola complex + SLNB + radiotherapy (or mastectomy + SLNB), then endocrine therapy. 441

DCIS

  • Non-invasive precursor; often non-palpable, found as microcalcifications on screening mammography → biopsy. Treatment: local excision if suitable, mastectomy if extensive; excellent prognosis.
  • DCIS (calcifications) → lumpectomy + radiotherapy. 441
  • Paget disease of the nipple = a superficial manifestation of an underlying breast cancer (eczema-like nipple change → biopsy). 426

Axillary surgery

  • ALND: removes ~20–30 nodes; needed for gross nodal disease; lymphedema up to ~40%, shoulder dysfunction.
  • SLNB: first draining node(s), usually ~3 nodes; radioactive tracer + blue dye → gamma probe; ± frozen section. Lymphedema ~3–4%. A blue/hot node is the sentinel, not necessarily malignant.
Choose SLNB unless the axilla is grossly involved.
  • Purpose of sentinel node biopsy → assess the extent of lymphatic involvement (staging the axilla). 441

Other points

  • Interval cancer: diagnosed between two screening mammograms (~10–15%) — not automatically an error.
  • Genetic (BRCA) testing — targeted: age < 50, triple-negative, male breast cancer, breast + ovarian family pattern.
  • BRCA1 is associated with breast (and ovarian) cancer. 437 ×4
  • Screening: goal = detect cancer before it is palpable (DCIS/microcalcifications). Average risk ~40–50 to ~75 (national program); high risk earlier (~30).
  • Breast MRI — young patients, implants, before/after neoadjuvant chemo, BRCA/high risk, when mammogram/US are insufficient.
  • Complications of breast/axillary surgery: bleeding, infection, seroma, shoulder dysfunction, numbness, lymphedema.
  • Chemo response is judged after starting treatment (clinical/imaging) — there is no test dose.
